Schwab says one hallmark is volume rising with no rise in price. On a chart the word has nothing to do with dividends. It is not a crash either: the price barely moves while the shares change hands. Heavy volume with no price progress is a warning. Someone may be selling quietly.

lesson_text: Log scale. A log scale measures moves in percent. $10 to $20 is a 100% gain, while $70 to $80 is a much smaller one. On long charts and big movers, use log scale. Percent is what your account feels.

answer_json.answer: Buying a pullback that holds a gap

lesson_text: Buying a pullback that holds a gap. The stock gaps up and runs, then comes back to the gap and holds. We buy the close as it holds. The stop is the gap top or the day's low, whichever is lower. If it drifts sideways at the gap, the stop tightens to just under the gap top. It is not buying the open of a fresh gap, and it does not wait for the gap to fill. Gap Support: the gap holds, you buy, and the gap is your line.

lesson_text: A loss hurts more than an equal gain. The Nobel summary of Kahneman's work says most people are more averse to losses than partial to gains of the same size. Fidelity says losses hurt more than equivalent gains feel good. How much more is debated: Investopedia notes some studies question the common 'about twice' figure. answer_json.answer: Review if it fits this market

lesson_text: Review if it fits this market. Steenbarger sees traders forget to update their playbooks when market conditions change. Fidelity says a plan can be amended over time as market conditions change. Review does not mean delete: a year of evidence may still hold when the market steadies. It also does not mean trading it bigger, or trading on with no check at all. A play that fits one market can sit out the next. Review it, don't force it.

choices: Keep trading it the same way
Trade it bigger to make it back
Review if it fits this market
prompt_json.q: What do you do with the playbook?
prompt_json.story: A setup in your playbook worked all year in a steady uptrend. The market turns choppy and the setup fails five times in two weeks.

deeper.trap: Two opposite mistakes pull at you here. One is to throw out a setup after a short losing run. Yet even a 60% win rate, which Steenbarger calls quite good, brings several losses in a row many times a year. The other is to keep firing it into a market it was never built for. Steenbarger's answer is review: update the playbook when market conditions change.

lesson_text: None of it stops every loss. It cuts down the impulsive ones.

prompt_json.q: Before the trade
steps: A trading plan is your rules for buying and selling, written before any money is on the line.
Your watchlist holds the stocks that meet your criteria. Entry and exit rules say when you get in and out.
A routine is the same prep every morning: the data out before the open, the index charts, your list.
None of it stops every loss. It cuts down the impulsive ones.

prompt_json.q: The numbers
steps: Win rate is how often you win. On its own it says little.
Put it next to your average win and average loss. Expectancy combines them: your average result per trade.
Profit factor is gross profit over gross loss. Over 1, the winners paid for the losers.
Judge none of it on a handful of trades. A small sample can fool you.
